title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
spaceBreakdown:
- vector<int> tails: up to n entries → O(n)  
- recursion depth: none  
- not counted: input vector, returned int
approach: Observe that for each possible length k of an increasing subsequence we only need the smallest possible last element; any larger last element can never lead to a longer subsequence. We keep these minima in a vector and update it with binary search as we scan the array. This “patience‑sorting” style method yields the length of the longest increasing subsequence in O(n log n) time and O(n) extra space, and its correctness follows from the invariant that the vector’s i‑th entry is the minimal tail of an increasing subsequence of length i+1.
hints:
If you already have an increasing subsequence, what property of its last element decides whether a later array value can extend it?  
The array length can be up to 2500.

Maintain a vector that stores the smallest possible tail for each subsequence length and update it with binary search.  
Example: processing the element 5 after having tails [2,3,7,101] replaces 7, giving [2,3,5,101].

for each x in nums  
 pos = lower_bound(tails, x)  
 if pos == end of tails push x  
 else *pos = x  
return size of tails

**All equal** - every element is the same, so the LIS length is 1.  
`Input: [7,7,7,7]` → `Expected: 1`  
⚠️ Bug: using `upper_bound` instead of `lower_bound` → returns 4  

**Strictly decreasing** - no element can follow another, LIS length is 1.  
`Input: [9,5,3,1]` → `Expected: 1`  
⚠️ Bug: updating with `*it = x` only when `it == end` (ignoring replacement) → returns 4  

**Negative numbers** - algorithm must work with values < 0.  
`Input: [-3,-1,-2,0]` → `Expected: 3` (subsequence [-3,-2,0])  
⚠️ Bug: initializing `tails` with a sentinel like `0` and comparing with `>` → returns 2  

**Single element** - trivial case, answer is 1.  
`Input: [42]` → `Expected: 1`  
⚠️ Bug: assuming `nums` has at least two elements and accessing `nums[1]` → runtime error

followUps.q: How would you modify the algorithm to also reconstruct one longest increasing subsequence, not just its length?
followUps.a: Keep an additional array `prev` storing the index of the predecessor for each element and another array `idx` storing the index of the element that gave the current tail. After processing, backtrack from the index of the last tail to build the subsequence. Time stays O(n log n); extra space becomes O(n).

followUps.q: What if the input size were up to 10⁵ and the numbers could be as large as 10⁹, but you were only allowed O(1) extra memory besides the input array?
followUps.a: You could perform the same patience‑sorting idea in‑place by overwriting the input array with the tail values, since only the tails are needed. This still runs in O(n log n) time and uses O(1) additional space.

followUps.q: Suppose the array is given as a stream (you cannot store all elements) and you need the length of the LIS after the whole stream is processed.
followUps.a: The same tail‑vector approach works because it only needs to keep the current tails; you can maintain this vector while reading each element from the stream. The algorithm remains O(n log n) time and O(k) space, where k is the length of the LIS (≤ n).
